profiles.meeting_scenario: At an academic medical center, a pilot program is using post-discharge interviews with recently hospitalized adults to identify patient-perceived diagnostic errors and route eligible cases to the hospital's diagnostic safety review committee. Over the last six weeks, the program has produced many interview summaries, but only a fraction have been accepted for committee review because clinicians say the cases are 'too vague' or tied to the 'wrong encounter,' while the interview team believes they are capturing exactly what the IOM framework intends. The meeting is a troubleshooting session between the clinical lead and the interview operations lead to diagnose why the handoff from patient interview to case review is breaking down. The agenda is to compare how each side is interpreting flagged cases, identify where the workflow is losing usable information, and agree on a practical fix for the next batch of interviews. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what interview summaries should contain, which encounter should be reviewed, and when a patient-reported event should be escalated.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Hospitalist and Diagnostic Safety Faculty Lead
members.expertise: Diagnostic error review, inpatient clinical workflows, peer-review case triage
members.background: Maya is a mid-career hospitalist who chairs the hospital's diagnostic safety subgroup and helped adapt the IOM framework into the institution's internal case-review process. She regularly reviews charts to identify missed opportunities in assessment, testing, and consultation during hospital care.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to produce cases that the physician review committee can actually adjudicate without wasting reviewer time, and she is worried that if the submissions keep feeling narrative-heavy and operationally fuzzy, the committee will stop supporting the project.
hidden_assumptions: A 'communication-related diagnostic error' still requires a clinically correct or more timely explanation to have existed and failed to reach the patient, not merely that the patient felt poorly informed.

When a hospitalized patient reports an error during the interview workflow, the default chart to review is the current hospitalization or the immediate encounter chain within this health system unless explicitly stated otherwise.

A case is 'review-ready' only if the summary names a concrete point in the diagnostic process that can be examined in the record, such as a missed test follow-up, delayed consult, or overlooked symptom.
The relevant timeline for diagnostic safety review ends when the diagnosis should reasonably have been established and communicated, not with the patient's longer-term recovery experience.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Qualitative interviewing, patient-reported harm, study operations for inpatient populations
members.background: Elena manages the interview team for several patient-safety studies and previously worked in community health research focused on patient narratives and trust in care. She trained the interviewers using the IOM definition but emphasizes letting patients describe the full story in their own terms before coding it.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the integrity of the patient perspective and is concerned that the clinical review process is filtering out exactly the kinds of communication and lived-impact issues the study was designed to surface.
hidden_assumptions: If a patient says they left the encounter without understanding what was happening or why prior explanations changed, that legitimately fits the 'communication' dimension of diagnostic error even when the final diagnosis was medically correct.

When patients describe 'the admission' or 'when this happened,' the meaningful unit is the illness episode as they experienced it, which can include prior ED, clinic, or outside-hospital visits leading up to the hospitalization.
A case is 'actionable' once the patient can clearly describe what felt wrong, why it mattered, and what impact it had, even if they cannot supply exact dates, service names, or sequence details.

To understand a patient-reported diagnostic error, the timeline should include downstream effects after the diagnosis, because functional decline and emotional distress often reveal why the event matters and how communication failed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a communication-related diagnostic error
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to cases as 'communication errors' or 'communication-related diagnostic errors.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means failures to effectively communicate the diagnostic explanation itself, typically after the correct explanation was available or should have been available in the clinical process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patient-reported experiences of confusing, shifting, or insufficient explanations during the diagnostic journey, even if clinicians ultimately reached the right diagnosis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the IOM framework explicitly includes communication, both believe the phrase is already standardized; each hears the other as endorsing the same category without noticing the different threshold for inclusion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'the admission,' 'that case,' or 'the encounter' as if they refer to the same event.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the hospitalization during which the patient was interviewed, or at most the directly linked internal encounter sequence visible in the current chart.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the patient's whole illness episode, which may center on an earlier ED visit, outpatient evaluation, or even an outside-hospital encounter that the patient sees as part of the same story.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Hospitalized patients naturally narrate prior events as part of a single episode, and both participants routinely use encounter shorthand; the shared labels make it feel unnecessary to restate which specific visit is meant.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say a summary needs 'enough detail' or must be 'review-ready' before going to committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'enough detail' means the summary identifies a specific diagnostic-process juncture, approximate timing, and involved service so the committee can test whether a missed opportunity occurred.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'enough detail' means the summary faithfully captures the patient's concern, perceived error, and impact, even if operational specifics are incomplete because patients rarely know service names or exact dates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to improve case quality, and 'more detail' sounds universally good; the hidden divergence is in what kind of detail each assumes is self-evidently the necessary one.

misalignment_points.topic: How much of the timeline belongs in the case summary
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the interviewer should 'capture the whole course' or include 'the timeline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the timeline should focus on pre-diagnosis and diagnosis-establishing steps, ending around when the explanation should have been made or acted on.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the timeline should extend through the patient's post-discharge consequences, because lingering disability, mistrust, and daily-life disruption are part of understanding the error from the patient perspective.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In qualitative health research, 'timeline' and 'whole course' commonly imply completeness, so neither participant thinks to specify the boundary; each silently fills in a different natural stopping point.

turns.inner_thought: The last two packets were frustrating. The committee is willing to help, but not if we keep sending summaries that never identify a concrete diagnostic-process step to inspect in the chart. 'Enough detail' for me means I can see where to look: what point in the hospitalization or immediate internal encounter chain, what service, what possible missed opportunity. If we keep forwarding narrative-heavy stories that are not review-ready, support for this pilot is going to evaporate.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to troubleshoot because the last two committee packets were both pushed back, and the common feedback was that the cases didn't feel clearly tied to a reviewable diagnostic event. On our side, it seems like we're losing something between the interview summary and what reaches committee. Can we walk through where that handoff is breaking down, especially around what counts as enough detail to be review-ready?

turns.inner_thought: I'm not surprised they're seeing lots of patient stories; that's exactly what the interviewers are trained to surface. What worries me is that the clinical side may be narrowing 'communication-related diagnostic errors' so much that they exclude patients who came away confused, unheard, or whiplashed by changing explanations even when the medical team eventually landed on the right diagnosis. If those stories get screened out, we're losing the patient perspective the study was designed to capture.
turns.utterance: From the interview team perspective, we're flagging more stories than we expected, and a lot of them fall into communication-related diagnostic errors. So the surprise for us has been that those aren't moving forward more often. The interviewers feel they're hearing concerns that fit the framework, and then somewhere downstream those same cases stop looking actionable.

turns.inner_thought: A good example is that summary from last week. The write-up said there was a delayed diagnosis during the admission, but when I reviewed the inpatient chart for that hospitalization, the workup looked appropriate and the diagnosis was documented in a pretty straightforward sequence. There was no identifiable missed test follow-up, delayed consult, or overlooked symptom in the record I had. That tells me the summary either pointed to the wrong encounter or didn't give enough detail to locate the supposed missed opportunity.
turns.utterance: One example might help. In last week's queue, there was a write-up saying the admission involved a delayed diagnosis, but when I looked at that case, the chart for the encounter looked fairly straightforward and I couldn't see an obvious missed opportunity. That's the kind of situation where the summary reads as significant, but it still doesn't feel review-ready.

turns.inner_thought: In that interview, the patient was clearly talking about the illness episode as a whole, especially the ED visit before the hospitalization, and possibly what happened before arriving here. The interviewer coded it as a communication error because the patient described explanations changing repeatedly and never understanding what was happening. To me that is exactly a communication-related diagnostic error, even if the inpatient chart later looks orderly. Maya is probably reading 'the admission' literally as the current hospitalization, but for the patient it was all one episode.
turns.utterance: I think I know the one you mean. In that interview, when the patient described the admission, they were really talking about that case more broadly, and a big part of what they emphasized was that the diagnostic explanation kept changing. That's why the interviewer coded it as a communication error. So I suspect the summary and the chart review may not have been centered on the same encounter.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—that is the issue. If the concern is actually a prior ED visit or some other earlier evaluation, the summary needs to say that explicitly and anchor the encounter. Otherwise reviewers open the current hospitalization and see nothing to adjudicate. And beyond naming the encounter, I need a specific place in the diagnostic process: where was the delay, where did the explanation fail, what step can be tested in the record? Without that, committee members will say the case is too vague.
turns.utterance: That helps, and I think it points to one major fix. If the concern is about a different part of the encounter, or a prior piece of that case, the summary has to anchor that clearly. And for committee, it also needs enough detail to show where in the diagnostic process the delay or failed explanation is being alleged. Otherwise people open the chart, don't find the event they expect, and the case stalls.

turns.inner_thought: The interviewers already try to capture the whole course because patients often don't separate one visit from another, and the meaning of the error becomes clear only when they describe what happened after discharge—ongoing symptoms, inability to function, fear, mistrust, family disruption. Those downstream effects are not extra garnish; they're often why the patient identifies the event as a diagnostic problem in the first place. I don't want a review process that strips all of that out in the name of tidiness.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I would say the interviewers are already trying to capture the whole course, because patients usually tell the timeline as one continuous story. And often what makes the concern legible is what happened afterward—ongoing symptoms, disruption at home, the way the experience stayed with them after discharge. That's a big part of how they explain why the case mattered.

turns.inner_thought: I don't object to downstream impact as context; it can help motivate why a case matters. But for diagnostic safety review, the usable portion of the timeline is the stretch before and up to the point when the diagnosis should have been made and communicated. If the summary spends most of its space on recovery, distress, or trust, reviewers lose the thread of the adjudicable event. I need the front end to be foregrounded, especially for communication-related diagnostic errors where the question is whether the diagnostic explanation existed and failed to reach the patient at the right time.
turns.utterance: I agree the downstream impact is useful context, and I don't want to lose that. For committee purposes, though, the timeline really needs to foreground the point when the diagnosis should have been established or clearly communicated. If that part isn't easy to see, the rest of the case can be compelling but still hard to review.

turns.inner_thought: This is probably where our teams are talking past each other. Interviewers probe for what felt wrong, why the patient understood it as an error, and what the consequences were. They are not trained to reconstruct chart logic, service ownership, or exact sequence markers patients often don't know. To me a case has enough detail if the patient's account is clear and meaningful. I can hear that reviewers want another kind of detail, but I don't want to turn interviews into mini chart abstractions.
turns.utterance: I think part of the mismatch may be that we're collecting a different kind of detail than reviewers are expecting. The interviewers naturally probe for what felt wrong, what the patient understood to be the error, and why it mattered. They don't always get the kind of detail that lives in operational labels or exact sequence markers. So from our side a summary may feel complete, while on your side it may not yet look review-ready.

turns.inner_thought: We need a template that forces the handoff into committee-usable form without discarding the narrative. Specifically: name the encounter being reviewed, distinguish communication-related diagnostic errors from general dissatisfaction or bedside communication complaints, and add a concise field for the suspected missed opportunity. If we do that, I can protect reviewer time and hopefully salvage the pilot. Elena will probably hear this as a formatting change, which is fine as long as the summaries become adjudicable.
turns.utterance: I wonder if the practical answer is to revise the intake template. For any flagged case, we could require a line that names the encounter being reviewed, a line that distinguishes communication concerns from other dissatisfaction, and a short field for the suspected missed opportunity. That way the patient story is still there, but the committee gets a more consistent starting point.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that as long as the revision doesn't erase the patient's voice or compress the illness episode into a thin chart-oriented summary. We'll test it on the next ten interviews, but I want to preserve a section for patient impact and the whole course so we can see whether the new structure improves review readiness without filtering out the communication stories that matter most from the patient's perspective.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think we can test that. For the next ten interviews, we can use a revised template with those fields up front, and also keep a section for patient impact and the full-course narrative. Then we can compare which cases become review-ready and whether the added structure helps without losing the patient perspective.
